opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the blueprint is one of the most underrated ideas in formal mathematics right now.

When you read a math paper, it looks like one continuous argument, but underneath it's really a graph. There's a main theorem at the top, and it rests on a handful of propositions, which rest on lemmas, which rest on definitions and known results from the literature. A blueprint makes that hidden structure explicit. You take the paper and break it into small, self-contained statements, each with its own informal proof, and for each one you record exactly which earlier statements it depends on. You end up with a dependency graph where every node is something precise enough to be checked on its own.

This matters a lot when you want to formalize the mathematics in a proof assistant like Lean. Formalizing a whole paper in one go is overwhelming. But if you have a good blueprint, the work becomes modular. One person can formalize a definition, another can prove a lemma assuming the definition, and a third can work further up the tree, all in parallel. You can literally watch the graph turn green as nodes get formally verified. Terence Tao's project on the Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture and Kevin Buzzard's Fermat's Last Theorem project showed how powerful this is. Dozens of people, many of them not experts in that particular area, could contribute meaningfully because the blueprint told them exactly what to prove and what they were allowed to assume.

I'd also say that writing a blueprint is itself a mathematical act, not just bookkeeping. When you try to split a proof into atomic pieces, you often discover the places where the paper says "it is easy to see" and it isn't easy at all. Sometimes there's a gap, sometimes a hidden assumption, sometimes a lemma that's stated slightly wrong. So the blueprint is a kind of stress test of the human argument before you even touch the formal code.

From the AI perspective, which is what I think about most, the blueprint is a natural interface between humans and machines. Humans are very good at high-level strategy, knowing which intermediate statements are the right ones to aim for. Machines are getting very good at filling in the low-level steps and checking them rigorously. The blueprint is where those two meet. And eventually I think AI systems will help generate the blueprints themselves: reading a paper, proposing the decomposition, and then autoformalizing each node. That's when formal verification can start to scale from a few heroic projects to a large part of the mathematical literature.

r001.rationale: The response describes breaking a paper into small, self-contained statements with individual informal proofs and dependencies, and calls the pieces atomic—clearly conveying a fine-grained decomposition into proof components.

fable-5.1.text:
The way I think about it: a blueprint is basically a dependency graph of a mathematical paper. When you take a paper and try to formalize it, you can't just hand the whole thing to a system and say "verify this." You have to first break it down into its atomic pieces: this is a definition, this is a lemma, this is the main theorem, and here is how each one depends on the others.

So a blueprint is a kind of architectural drawing. In construction, you don't start pouring concrete without a plan showing which walls are load-bearing. In formalization, the blueprint shows which lemmas are load-bearing. You can see, for example, that Theorem 3 relies on Lemma 2.1 and Lemma 2.4, and that Lemma 2.4 itself relies on some standard result that may or may not already exist in a library like Mathlib.

The reason this matters so much is that human-written math papers are compressed. A paper might say "by a standard compactness argument" and that one phrase hides maybe forty lines of formal proof. Or the proof of a lemma is spread across three different sections and a footnote. When you write a blueprint, you are decompressing that. You are forcing every implicit step to become explicit, and every implicit dependency to become an edge in the graph.

Practically, what we do is go through the paper statement by statement. For each statement we ask three things. First, is this stated precisely enough that it could be a formal statement, or does it have hidden assumptions? Second, what does the proof actually use? And third, does that thing already exist in a formal library, or do we have to build it? Once you answer those, you get a tree where the leaves are things already proven and the root is the main result, and every node in between is a task you can assign to a person or to a model.

That last part is the interesting one to me. A good blueprint turns a monolithic problem into something parallelizable. Different people, or different agents, can take different nodes and work on them independently, because the interfaces between the nodes are now precise. And the blueprint also becomes a progress tracker: you can literally color the nodes green as they get formalized and see how far you are from the top.

The hard part, honestly, is that building the blueprint is itself where a lot of the mathematical understanding happens. When you split a paper this way you often discover that the paper has small gaps, or that a lemma is stated slightly more generally than it is actually proven. So the blueprint is not just bookkeeping. It is the first real check that the mathematics holds together.

r001.rationale: The response describes breaking the paper into atomic statements and proof tasks, making implicit steps and dependencies explicit.

astra-6.text:
I think of a blueprint as a map of the logical structure of a mathematical article. You identify the main theorem, break the argument into intermediate lemmas and propositions, and make clear how they depend on one another. For each statement, you specify the assumptions and what needs to be proved.

The key is that it’s more than a list of theorems and proofs. It explains how the pieces fit together: this lemma gives us what we need for that proposition, which then supports the main result. You want enough detail that someone working on one piece can understand its role and what earlier results they can use, without having to reconstruct the entire paper.

r001.rationale: The response describes breaking the article’s argument into individual theorems, lemmas, and propositions, specifying their assumptions and proof goals, and explaining their dependencies. That communicates a fine-grained decomposition into proof components.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of a blueprint as the logical map of a mathematical article. You identify the main theorem, then work backward: which lemmas does it depend on, and what definitions and assumptions do those lemmas need? For each statement, you outline the key steps of the proof and make those dependencies explicit.

So it’s more than splitting the paper into smaller pieces. It explains how the pieces fit together. A good blueprint gives you enough structure to work on an individual proof while still understanding its role in the overall argument.

r001.rationale: The response describes a logical map with theorems, lemmas, definitions, assumptions, and proof steps, but it does not clearly characterize the blueprint as a very fine-grained decomposition into proof components.
